name: Disseminated (Miliary) Tuberculosis

pathogens.why: Disseminated TB reflects hematogenous spread of M. tuberculosis, classically producing miliary lung nodules and multi-organ involvement (liver, spleen, bone marrow, CNS), and is disproportionately seen in immunocompromised hosts (HIV, malnutrition, immunosuppressive therapy) where the presentation can be especially non-specific, contributing to diagnostic delay.

investigations.why: Classic miliary pattern (diffuse small nodules) supports the diagnosis, though it may be subtle or absent early.

investigations.test: Blood culture for mycobacteria (if available) and AFB smear of any accessible fluid/tissue
investigations.why: May provide microbiological confirmation; mycobacterial blood culture has reasonable yield in disseminated disease, particularly in HIV co-infection.

investigations.test: Liver or bone marrow biopsy (if hepatosplenomegaly/cytopenias and other tests inconclusive)
investigations.why: Can provide histological confirmation (caseating granulomas, AFB on staining) when other less invasive tests are unrevealing.
Essential given the strong association between disseminated TB and immunosuppression, with direct treatment implications.
Screens for concurrent CNS involvement, which would extend treatment duration.

references: National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) India Guidelines
reason: Prolonged unexplained fever with weight loss, night sweats, and hepatosplenomegaly, particularly in an immunocompromised host, raises significant suspicion for disseminated (miliary) tuberculosis. Given the high mortality of untreated disseminated TB and the often non-specific presentation delaying diagnosis, a low threshold for starting empiric antitubercular therapy is appropriate after reasonable attempts at microbiological/histological confirmation, rather than waiting for definitive proof in a deteriorating patient.

clinicalPearls: Presentation is notoriously nonspecific and protean, varying with the organs predominantly seeded; constitutional features (fever, night sweats, anorexia, weakness, weight loss) dominate in most patients (Harrison 22e p.1390).

Choroidal tubercles on fundoscopic eye examination are pathognomonic of miliary TB and are present in up to roughly 30% of cases, so dilated fundoscopy is a high-yield bedside step (Harrison 22e p.1390).
A high index of suspicion is essential; the diagnosis is easily missed and untreated miliary TB is lethal, whereas early treatment is curative (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Sputum-smear microscopy is negative in most cases, so a negative smear does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1390).
The tuberculin skin test may be negative in up to half of patients, with reactivity sometimes returning during chemotherapy; a negative TST therefore cannot rule out disease (Harrison 22e p.1390).
In adults miliary TB may arise from either recent infection or reactivation of old disseminated foci, whereas in children it more often follows primary infection (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Granulomas are often found on liver or bone-marrow biopsy, and bronchoalveolar lavage with transbronchial biopsy improves bacteriologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1390).
harrison.pathophysiology: Miliary/disseminated TB results from hematogenous spread of M. tuberculosis when an acquired immune response fails to contain infection. Bacilli carried to regional lymph nodes reach the central venous return and the systemic circulation, seeding multiple organs with innumerable small (1-2 mm) yellowish granulomas resembling millet seeds. Occult hematogenous dissemination commonly follows primary infection; in the very young and the immunocompromised (including people living with HIV), insufficient immunity allows progression to fatal miliary disease or tuberculous meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1386, 1390).
infectionMimics: Disseminated fungal infection (a differential when miliary or interstitial pulmonary infiltrates and multi-organ involvement are present) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundoscopic eye examination for choroidal tubercles (pathognomonic, up to ~30% of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy for improved bacteriologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1390)

Full blood count for hematologic clues (anemia with leukopenia, lymphopenia, neutrophilic leukocytosis/leukemoid reactions, polycythemia; pancytopenia in nonreactive form; DIC reported) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Liver function tests including alkaline phosphatase (elevated with hepatic involvement) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Tuberculin skin test (may be falsely negative in up to half of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1390)
Xpert MTB/RIF as the initial test when TB meningitis is suspected; positive results prompt immediate treatment (Harrison 22e p.1393)
redFlags: Meningismus, present in fewer than 10% of cases, signals possible concurrent tuberculous meningitis and warrants urgent CNS evaluation (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Pancytopenia with an acute septicemic course suggests nonreactive miliary TB, a rare and rapidly fatal form from massive dissemination (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Disseminated intravascular coagulation has been reported and indicates severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1390).
harrison.prognosis: Unrecognized miliary TB is lethal, but with proper early treatment it is amenable to cure. Cryptic miliary TB (seen in the elderly) runs a chronic course with mild intermittent fever and anemia, ultimately progressing to meningeal involvement before death. The nonreactive (acute septicemic) form is rapidly fatal with multiple necrotic, nongranulomatous lesions at postmortem. Glucocorticoid therapy has not proved beneficial in miliary TB (Harrison 22e p.1390).
pitfalls: Relying on sputum-smear microscopy or the tuberculin skin test to exclude the diagnosis, since both are frequently negative in miliary TB (Harrison 22e p.1390).

Expecting a typical chest radiograph: early in the course, and especially among people living with HIV, the CXR may show no abnormality; findings may instead be large or interstitial infiltrates or pleural effusion rather than the classic miliary reticulonodular pattern (Harrison 22e p.1390).
Overlooking cryptic miliary TB in elderly patients with only mild intermittent fever and anemia (Harrison 22e p.1390).
